2026-03-18 15:30 UTC | Duration: ~75m | Attendees: Sofia Martinez (Redwood AE), Alex Chen (Redwood SE), Jamal Reed (observer), Dr. Priya Nair (Borealis Head of ML), Ethan Park (Infra), Maya Lopes (SRE)

Auto-summary (auto-generated): quick deep-dive, fairly technical.

00:00 Sofia (Redwood AE): hey everyone, thanks for joining, we got about 75 minutes, alex will lead the runtime profiling bits and i'll chime on pricing/next steps 

00:10 Priya (Borealis): yeah, thanks. Primary ask is predictable latency at 2k tokens and throughput for batch sizes up to 8, also we have KV-cache heavy workloads for inference-on-dialogue so curious about cache eviction, warm start, and cuda graphs warmup behavior.
00:22 Alex (Redwood SE): great, that's exactly what we prepared. quick agenda: kernel selection differences, cudagraphs and warmup, kv cache and batching interactions, quantization tradeoffs, then we'll look at some traces we captured on an A100. sound good?
00:30 Priya: yes.
01:05 Alex: first, kernel selection 





- TRT-LLM tends to pick fused kernels for attention and matmul that reduce memory bandwidth and lower latency for medium sequence lengths; vLLM/torch kernels are more general-purpose and sometimes fall back to multi-kernel paths, which can increase kernel launch overhead. you can see this in the cuda-prof output where TRT fuses softmax+matmul or uses optimized flash attention variants.
01:30 Ethan (Borealis): when you say fused, do you mean at runtime it picks a different operator implementation or it's compiled ahead-of-time?
01:40 Alex: a bit of both 

TRT-LLM uses TensorRT's engine building step to select kernels for given shapes and data types, so there's an engine generation/compile step; vLLM with custom kernels will choose kernels at runtime, sometimes JITing or selecting cuBLAS/cuDNN calls. that means TRT can be faster at steady state but has a longer cold start and engine rebuild time when sequence shapes or batch sizes change.
02:05 Maya (SRE): that cold-start overhead concerns us 

our infra scales up/down and we can't afford 10s of seconds per node. how big is the warmup for cuda graphs?
02:18 Alex: cuda graphs can help amortize launch overhead, but they need stable shapes; we saw in our tests that repeated calls with similar seq-len hit the cached cudagraph and latency drops by ~30-40% after warmup iterations. cold start to a fully warmed graph can be 5-20 iters depending on model size. the problem is variability: if your seq-len distribution is wide, graphs are less effective.
03:00 Priya: ok, what about KV cache 

does TRT-LLM keep it on GPU and how does that impact memory for big context windows?
03:12 Alex: both runtimes keep KV on GPU to avoid round trips. memory footprint scales with context length and hidden size; TRT's static planning can sometimes allocate more aggressive buffers for throughput, which may be higher peak memory but more efficient memory access patterns. vLLM's chunked cache and streaming approach sometimes uses less peak memory but higher per-token overhead. so there's a tradeoff: TRT can give lower per-token latency at the cost of higher peak memory.
03:48 Ethan: do you have numbers for 16k vs 4k contexts on A100?
03:55 Alex: in our internal runs, for 4k tokens TRT-LLM + FP16 + cudagraphs was giving 1.8x throughput vs vLLM baseline with similar latency at P50. At 16k, resource constraints push TRT to either reduce batch or fall back to fragmented kernels 

shrinking throughput advantage to ~1.1x and memory becomes binding. these are approximate; we'll share the raw traces.
04:30 Priya: and quantization? we are sensitive to minimal accuracy drift.
04:38 Alex: 8-bit quantization (INT8 or Q8 variants) with TRT gives big perf wins but requires calibration; post-training quant can introduce small perf regressions. 4-bit techniques are promising but model-dependent. vLLM supports quantized backends too, but you may see different rounding/accuracy profiles across libs. our recommendation: run evals on your prompt set and check logits drift / answer-level metrics.
05:10 Priya: ok, can you also explain batching strategy impact 

we often have many small conversational requests and occasional large batched scoring jobs.
05:22 Alex: yeah so continuous batching works well for small conversational workloads; the serving runtime can mesh requests to form micro-batches. TRT engines often prefer fixed batch shapes 

if you can pad to fixed small-batch sizes it helps. vLLM's dynamic batching handles heterogenous shapes better at the cost of more kernel launches. Our runtime supports hybrid approach: sticky small-batch routes for low-latency paths and batcher for high-throughput background scoring.
06:05 Ethan: what about VPC and on-prem, specifically KMS/HSM integrations? we need to keep model weights inside our network and limit outbound.
06:16 Sofia (AE): Redwood Private supports customer-managed control plane and KMS integration; you can host model weights in your VPC storage and we can deploy the inference nodes on-prem. we'll send the security pack but note TRT engine building may require ephemeral GPU-local scratch during compile. we can coordinate network policies so compile artifacts don't leak.
06:40 Priia: that's good. what about audits and logs?
06:45 Sofia: we provide audit logs and can integrate with your SIEM, plus SOC2 docs in the package we'll send.
07:10 Alex: i want to show a slice of a trace 

i'm going to read out a simplified cuda-prof snippet we captured on an A100 with a 2.7B model.
07:20 Alex: [shows snippet] you can see repeated small kernels at 200-400us each in vLLM, whereas TRT uses larger fused kernels at ~500-800us but fewer launches, so end-to-end latency is lower due to lower CPU-GPU syncs. there's also a spike where cudagraphs warm up 

first 8 calls show higher latency then steady-state.
08:05 Priya: are these numbers per-token or per-chunk?
08:10 Alex: per-token measured at generator step with a 1-token emission window 

so basically per-token generation step. in batched runs, the per-token time goes down because some operations amortize.
08:35 Maya: any known issues with cudagraphs + dynamic KV updates? like updating cache mid-graph?
08:42 Alex: yes, cudagraphs need predictable memory writes; if you mutate KV shapes mid-graph you break the graph and need re-graphing. we've implemented a layered approach: small dynamic writes occur in a separate kernel path while the main attention compute uses graphs; this keeps most benefits while allowing some dynamism, but it isn't free.
09:10 Priya: that sounds complex. what's the operational implication for our SREs?
09:18 Maya: (laughs) yes please be blunt.
09:20 Alex: operationally: expect a testing matrix 

- different seq-lens, batch sizes, and quant modes. TRT deployments usually prefer slightly more capacity headroom and scheduled warmup jobs to keep graphs cached. vLLM is more forgiving to variable traffic but can incur higher per-token cost.
09:50 Ethan: how about fallbacks 

- if TRT engine fails on a rare shape do you auto-fallback to vLLM-compatible kernels?
10:00 Alex: we support fallback policies: automatic fallback to a generic runtime path or to a compatibility engine. you can configure latency SLO-based fallback or cost-based. Fallback adds complexity but increases resilience.
10:30 Priia: can you explain the engineer-level steps to reproduce the benchmark on our side?
10:38 Alex: sure 

we'll provide a runnable script that: pulls model artifact (or use your own weights), runs engine build for TRT with specified shapes, runs vLLM baseline with same seeds, captures nvprof/cuda-memcheck and cudagraph traces, and exports a CSV with per-step latencies and mem usage. we'll include a guidance doc for calibration and eval prompts.
11:10 Priia: perfect. what about model variants 

we have some finetuned weights and some LLMs with custom kernels (sparse attention). any gotchas?
11:20 Alex: sparse or custom ops may not be supported by TensorRT and would require custom plugins; that can increase compile/engine work. vLLM may support them more directly via PyTorch kernels but at perf cost. we'll capture those in pre-onboarding checks.
11:55 Jamal (observer): quick note 

- when you do the benchmark please collect tail latencies (P95-P99) and memory peaks per node, those matter for infra sizing.
12:10 Sofia: good point. we'll include that in the spreadsheet.
